title: Generalized Intention Modeling in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
claim: Several intent encoders feed a learned gating mixture into one adaptive representation, with auxiliary decoders used only during training.
layout: 1 panel, top-to-bottom, parallel encoder columns, row labels at left, brackets at right
description: A vertical architecture diagram with stage labels down the left side: ego-agent input, encoder, latent embedding, projection layer, projected embedding, gating layer, aggregate embedding, and policy. A wide input box at the top, (o_t^1, a_{t-1}^1), feeds three parallel columns. Each column has an encoder (f^a, f^o, f^(...)), a blue latent embedding z, a projection layer p, and a blue projected embedding e. Dashed grey decoder boxes h branch off the latents and predict a, o and y. This branch is marked 'Training only'. A wide gating box g spans all columns, then a softmax weight formula and a weighted-sum formula lead to a blue aggregate embedding z^MIX. That embedding feeds the policy π^1, which also receives the ego input through a long feedback line on the left. Right-hand curly brackets mark which parts are trained by their own auxiliary loss and which are trained end-to-end with the policy. Grey and blue fills on a white background. The eye goes first to the top box and then down the columns to z^MIX.
caption: Overview of the \mixer{} architecture. Encoders $\{f^k\}_{k=1}^K$ produce latent representations that are combined via an MoE module into an adaptive opponent representation $z^{\mixer}$. Decoders $h^k$ and their predictions are used only during training and discarded at execution, following CTDE.
abstract: Modeling an opponent's intent is critical for effective decision-making in non-cooperative, competitive, and general-sum multi-agent reinforcement learning. Existing opponent modeling methods encode intent using an embedding derived from episode information chosen a priori, such as the opponent's next action or a future environment state, and use this to guide the ego-agent's behavior. These approaches assume that the chosen information is universally representative of intent; however, we show empirically that this is not the case as intentions are often task- and environment-dependent. To address this, we introduce a task-adaptive opponent modeling framework that learns a performance-driven mixture of multiple intent representations. We further introduce a new intention representation that maximizes mutual information with the ego-agent's future returns, thereby capturing opponent information that is most directly relevant to performance. Our approach consistently matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art baselines across diverse tasks and yields insights into when and why different opponent modeling strategies succeed.
